prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

Ay, gaze upon her rose-wreathed hair, And gaze upon her smile; Seem as you drank the very air Her breath perfumed the while: And wake for her the gifted line, That wild and witching lay, And swear your heart is as a shrine, That only owns her sway. ’Tis well: I am revenged at last,— Mark you that scornful cheek,— The eye averted as you pass’d, Spoke more than words could speak. Ay, now by all the bitter tears That I have shed for thee,— The racking doubts, the burning fears,— Avenged they well may be— By the nights pass’d in sleepless care, The days of endless woe; All that you taught my heart to bear, All that yourself will know. I would not wish to see you laid Within an early tomb; I should forget how you betray’d, And only weep your doom: But this is fitting punishment, To live and love in vain,— Oh my wrung heart, be thou content, And feed upon his pain. Go thou and watch her lightest sigh,— Thine own it will not be; And bask beneath her sunny eye,— It will not turn on thee. ’Tis well: the rack, the chain, the wheel, Far better hadst thou proved; Ev’n I could almost pity feel, For thou art not beloved.

prompts.L3:
Please expand the following bullet points into a complete, well-structured text:

- The speaker urges the man to admire and praise another woman as if wholly devoted to her.
- The speaker feels finally revenged after having suffered scorn, betrayal, sleepless nights, doubts, fears, and grief because of him.
- The speaker does not wish him dead, because death would soften her anger into pity and sorrow.
- The speaker sees his punishment as living and loving in vain, suffering the same unreturned love he caused her to endure.
- The poem ends with the speaker almost pitying him because the woman he loves does not return his affection.

prompts.L5:
Please write a text about the following topic:

Keywords: And, Seem, Her

outputs.L1:
Ay, gaze upon her rose-wreathed hair,  
And gaze upon her smile;  
Seem as you drank the very air  
Her breath perfumed the while.  

And wake for her the gifted line,  
That wild and witching lay,  
And swear your heart is as a shrine  
That only owns her sway.  

’Tis well: I am revenged at last—  
Mark you that scornful cheek;  
The eye averted as you passed  
Spoke more than words could speak.  

Ay, now, by all the bitter tears  
That I have shed for thee—  
The racking doubts, the burning fears—  
Avenged they well may be.  

By the nights passed in sleepless care,  
The days of endless woe;  
All that you taught my heart to bear,  
All that yourself will know.  

I would not wish to see you laid  
Within an early tomb;  
I should forget how you betrayed,  
And only weep your doom.  

But this is fitting punishment:  
To live and love in vain—  
Oh, my wrung heart, be thou content,  
And feed upon his pain.  

Go thou and watch her lightest sigh—  
Thine own it will not be;  
And bask beneath her sunny eye—  
It will not turn on thee.  

’Tis well: the rack, the chain, the wheel,  
Far better hadst thou proved;  
Ev’n I could almost pity feel,  
For thou art not beloved.
outputs.L2:
Yes—look at the roses twined in her hair,  
and look at the sweetness of her smile.  
Act as though the very air you breathe  
is made fragrant by her breath.  
Compose for her your finest verse,  
that strange, enchanting song,  
and vow that your heart is a sacred altar  
devoted to her alone.

Good—it is enough. I am avenged at last.  
Notice that proud, disdainful face:  
the way her eyes turned from you as you passed  
said more than any speech could say.  
Yes, by every bitter tear  
I have shed because of you,  
by every tormenting doubt  
and every feverish fear,  
my suffering may now be repaid.

By the nights I spent awake in anguish,  
by the days that seemed endless in grief,  
by all the pain you taught my heart to endure—  
pain you yourself will come to understand—  
this is justice.  
I would not want to see you dead too young,  
lying in an early grave;  
then I would forget your betrayal  
and mourn only your fate.

But this punishment is fitting:  
to go on living, and to love without return.  
O my bruised and suffering heart, be satisfied,  
and take nourishment from his misery.  
Go, then—watch for even her faintest sigh;  
it will never belong to you.  
Warm yourself beneath the brightness of her gaze;  
it will never be turned toward you.

It is well. The torture-rack, the chain, the wheel—  
you would have found them easier to bear.  
Even I could almost feel pity for you,  
because you are not loved.
outputs.L3:
The speaker urges the man to go on admiring and praising another woman, behaving as though he is entirely devoted to her. She encourages him to display his love openly, to worship this new woman, and to offer her all the compliments and affection he once denied or misused.

In doing so, the speaker feels that she is finally revenged. She remembers how much she suffered because of him: his scorn, his betrayal, her sleepless nights, and the constant doubts, fears, and grief that his actions caused her. For a long time, she endured the pain of loving someone who did not treat her faithfully or kindly. Now, seeing him caught in the same kind of emotional torment, she feels a sense of justice.

However, the speaker does not wish him dead. If he were to die, her anger would turn into pity and sorrow, and her desire for revenge would lose its force. Death would end his suffering too quickly and would make him an object of compassion rather than punishment.

Instead, she believes his true punishment is to live and to love in vain. He must experience the anguish of giving his heart to someone who does not return his affection. In this way, he is forced to suffer the same unrequited love and emotional distress that he once caused her to endure.

By the end of the poem, the speaker’s anger begins to soften. Although she has wanted revenge, she almost pities him because the woman he loves does not love him back. His pain mirrors her own past suffering, and this recognition brings the poem to a close with a mixture of satisfaction, bitterness, and reluctant compassion.
outputs.L4:
The poem explores the theme of revenge after betrayal through the speaker’s bitter and emotionally charged address to a former lover. The speaker appears to have been deeply hurt by someone who once received their love but failed to return it faithfully or sincerely. As a result, the poem is filled with resentment, grief, and a desire for justice. Rather than simply expressing sadness, the speaker turns their pain into a curse-like wish: they want the former lover to experience the same suffering they have endured.

A central part of the poem is its vivid imagery of unrequited devotion. The speaker presents love not as a gentle or joyful feeling, but as something painful, humiliating, and consuming when it is not returned. The former lover is imagined as being trapped in a situation where he gives his heart to someone who remains cold and indifferent. This mirrors the speaker’s own earlier experience and makes the punishment feel fitting. The imagery of scorn and emotional torment emphasizes how destructive unequal love can be, especially when one person is devoted while the other is careless or cruel.

The poem’s emotional force comes from the speaker’s mixture of heartbreak and satisfaction. Although the speaker has been wounded, they are not powerless. Through language, they create a form of revenge: the former lover will be made to suffer in exactly the way they made the speaker suffer. This reversal gives the poem a strong sense of poetic justice. The punishment is not physical or public, but deeply personal and emotional. The lover’s pain will come from loving someone who does not love him back, forcing him to understand the agony he once caused.

Ultimately, the poem suggests that betrayal leaves behind more than sorrow; it can also produce anger, bitterness, and a longing for retribution. The speaker’s wounded heart finds satisfaction in imagining the former lover’s future misery. By making his punishment a reflection of his own cruelty, the poem turns emotional suffering into justice. The result is a powerful portrayal of love turned into resentment, where revenge is achieved not through action, but through the hope that the betrayer will be forced to feel the pain of unreturned love.
outputs.L5: And though the world around her often seemed loud and uncertain, she carried a quiet strength within. People might seem to overlook her at first, but anyone who truly listened could hear the confidence in her voice and the kindness in her words. Her journey was not always easy, yet each step taught her something new about courage, patience, and hope.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a dramatic Romantic-era poem in an archaic style about a scorned lover taking revenge by watching their betrayer suffer unrequited love.
counterfactuals.output:
**The Vigil of the Scorned**

Lo! I have seen thee bow thy haughty head,  
Thou that didst laugh when mine was bent in dust;  
Thou that with roses lured my heart, then fled,  
And left it to the worm, the wind, the rust.  

I cursed thee not when first thy faith grew cold,  
Nor cried to Heaven for thunder on thy name;  
I only watched the sunset waste its gold,  
And fed my silence with a patient flame.  

For vengeance hath a slow and secret wing,  
And Time, the priest, prepares the bitter cup;  
The lips that once forswore are taught to cling,  
The eyes that scorned are lifted vainly up.  

Now art thou pale beneath another’s gaze,  
As I was pale beneath thy careless smile;  
Thy soul goes forth through solitary ways,  
And finds no hand to greet it mile on mile.  

She turneth from thee as thou turnedst from me,  
With silken words that wound yet leave no scar;  
Her heart, a moon upon a frozen sea,  
Shines cold and beautiful—and dwells afar.  

O sweeter far than wrath’s impetuous blade,  
Than midnight steel, or poison darkly poured,  
To mark thee in Love’s desolation laid,  
And hear thee call on one who hears no word!  

I sit unseen where cypress shadows creep,  
And watch thy proud despair make pact with night;  
Thou dost not know what ancient eyes still keep  
Their feast upon thy ruin and delight.  

Cry on!—thy cries are music to the dead  
Of all my hopes that withered at thy side;  
Each tear that falleth from thy sleepless bed  
Restores one jewel to my murdered pride.  

Yet think not I am wholly made of stone:  
There was a time my heart had bled for thine;  
But thou didst teach it how to beat alone,  
And changed its prayer to this austere design.  

Therefore, beloved once, be now accursed  
Not by my hand, but by thine own desire:  
Drink as I drank of love denied—and thirst,  
And warm thy phantom bosom at its fire.  

When thou art old, and beauty’s banners torn,  
When hope lies mute beneath the churchyard rain,  
Remember one who loved, was lost, was scorned—  
And smiled to see thee kneel to Love in vain.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a Victorian-style ballad with themes of jealousy, heartbreak, betrayal, and the bitter satisfaction of seeing an unfaithful beloved rejected.
counterfactuals.output:
**The Forsaken’s Ballad**

Upon the stair at Ravensmere,  
Where lamps burned wan and low,  
I watched my false love take her hand  
And whisper soft and slow.  

Her glove was white, her smile was bright,  
Her diamonds caught the flame;  
And every laugh she cast on him  
Fell on me like shame.  

“O love,” quoth I, “how lightly worn  
Are vows beneath the moon;  
The heart you swore should be your home  
You bartered ere the noon.”  

He turned aside, he knew me not,  
Though once he knelt to me;  
And she, with all her satin pride,  
Looked past me haughtily.  

I bore the wound as widows bear  
The tolling of a bell;  
I kept my tears behind my veil,  
And wished them both farewell.  

But time, that grave and patient clerk,  
Writes truth in ink of gall;  
The roses fled her painted cheek,  
The pearls began to fall.  

For she had heard, as I had heard,  
His vows were lightly made;  
And when she sought his faithless hand,  
He bowed—and turned away.  

He left her in the candle-glare,  
Alone amid the throng;  
The music faltered like a prayer,  
The night grew black and long.  

She stood where I had stood before,  
With wounded eyes cast down;  
No jewel then could hide her grief,  
No lace become a crown.  

And I, who once had cursed her name,  
Felt pity stir—and cease;  
For oh, there is a bitter wine  
That tastes at first like peace.  

I did not laugh, I did not speak,  
I only watched her learn  
How cold the ashes of a heart  
When love has ceased to burn.  

So let him roam from breast to breast,  
A moth to every light;  
The flame he steals shall scorch his wings  
Before the end of night.  

And if my soul still bears his mark,  
A scar no years remove,  
I thank the dark that showed me clear  
The poverty of love.  

For sweeter than his perjured kiss,  
And dearer than his sigh,  
Was seeing pride and treachery meet  
Beneath a stranger’s eye.  

Yet Heaven forgive this jealous heart,  
That found its solace there;  
A broken vow, a broken girl,  
A ballroom thick with prayer.  

The fiddles played, the candles died,  
The dawn crept pale and cold;  
And I went home with empty hands—  
But not so poor as old.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate a poem in the style of Letitia Elizabeth Landon, using elevated diction and rhymed stanzas, where the speaker addresses a former lover who now loves someone who does not love him back.
counterfactuals.output:
Thou turn’st from me—yet not to bliss,  
Not to the breast that answers thine;  
Thy cherished hope, thy dreamed-of kiss,  
Are laid upon a cold, proud shrine.  
I would not mock thy wasted vow,  
Though once thy faithless words were mine;  
There is a sorrow on thy brow  
Too much resembling what was mine.  

I see thee bend where she is bright,  
As pilgrims kneel to distant stars;  
Thou call’st her name through lonely night,  
And count’st thy heart by inward scars.  
She smiles—as summer smiles above  
The graves her careless roses dress;  
She takes the incense of thy love,  
And gives thee only loveliness.  

Ah! once for me thy accents woke  
Like music under moonlit skies;  
For me the tender falsehood spoke,  
The pleading hand, the lifted eyes.  
I deemed that truth in thee had birth,  
I made thy change my destiny;  
And learned how little love on earth  
Can hold a wandering heart like thee.  

Yet now, when I behold thee pine,  
Pale captive of another’s chain,  
I feel no triumph—grief like thine  
Has purified my own disdain.  
For tears, though bitterly they flow,  
Have something sacred in their fall;  
And they who best have known Love’s woe  
Are slow to scorn it most of all.  

Go—worship still that haughty beam  
Which warms thee not, yet keeps thee near;  
Go—feed upon the faithless dream,  
And call its poison sweet and dear.  
Perchance, when all thy hopes are past,  
When pride itself has ceased to save,  
Thou’lt learn what hearts may love steadfast—  
And what they lose beside a grave.  

Not mine the prayer to bid thee bleed,  
Nor mine the curse to seal thy doom;  
I would not have thy spirit feed  
On ashes, darkness, and the tomb.  
But if remembrance haunt thy sleep,  
And my name tremble through thy pain,  
Think—there was one who learned to weep,  
And loved thee once, and not in vain.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Create an old-fashioned lyrical poem beginning with “Ay, gaze upon her rose-wreathed hair,” and continue it as a revenge monologue from a wounded lover.
counterfactuals.output:
Ay, gaze upon her rose-wreathed hair,  
And mark the lilies at her breast;  
How meek she moves through perfumed air,  
How saintly seems her silken rest.  

Yet I, who kissed those hands of snow,  
Have felt their frost about my heart;  
I, only I, am sworn to know  
The viper hidden under art.  

She smiled—O Heaven!—as angels smile,  
And bade my foolish spirit rise;  
Then sold my peace with courtly guile,  
And turned to mock my darkened eyes.  

Go, tell her still the viols play,  
The lamps still crown her midnight feast;  
But somewhere waits a reckoning day,  
And I, her scorned and silent priest.  

I will not storm her gilded door,  
Nor stain with wrath her marble floor;  
No blade of mine shall seek her side,  
No hand of mine profane her pride.  

But I will live, and living, be  
A shadow at her bright renown;  
A whispered name across the lea,  
A thorn beneath her bridal crown.  

When flatterers kneel and swear her pure,  
My song shall wander through the hall;  
Its mournful truth shall long endure,  
And one by one her roses fall.  

For every vow she broke in jest,  
For every tear she left to burn,  
I’ll bind a verse about her breast  
And make the faithless world return.  

Let time, that gray and patient lord,  
Set dust upon her golden train;  
Let memory draw its quiet sword,  
And answer sweetness back with pain.  

Ay, let her dance where candles gleam,  
Let young hearts perish in her glance;  
I walk beside her like a dream,  
The ghost that waits beyond the dance.  

And when at last her mirror shows  
No queen, but winter’s borrowed face,  
She’ll seek among her faded rose  
One petal of my vanished grace.  

Then shall she know what love became  
When mercy starved and hope was slain:  
Not fire, not blood, not open flame—  
But song, immortal with disdain.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a gothic Romantic monologue in verse where the narrator says they do not wish death on the person who betrayed them, only the punishment of living and loving in vain.
counterfactuals.output:
I do not call the grave to take thee down,  
Nor bid the worms make banquet of thy name;  
Let no black bell be shaken in the town,  
Let no cold priest lean muttering o’er thy shame.  

Live—live beneath the moon’s accusing eye,  
Where ruined towers rake the storm apart,  
And every wind that wanders, wandering by,  
Shall find my whisper buried in thy heart.  

Live, and be beautiful when dawn is pale;  
Live, and be praised by mouths that do not know  
How deep a dagger hides beneath a veil,  
How sweetly roses over poison grow.  

I would not have thee sleep in marble peace,  
With folded hands absolved of all desire;  
No—let thy restless pulse have no release,  
Let blood remember what it dared conspire.  

Love, as I loved, with famine in the soul;  
Stretch out thy arms to phantoms in the rain;  
Press burning lips to shadows, and the whole  
Wide world give back no answer but thy pain.  

May every face that kindles at thy gaze  
Turn from thee when thy hope is most complete;  
May every vow dissolve in mist and haze,  
May honey change to ashes on thy sweet.  

Not death—too soft a cloak, too still a bed,  
Too kind a dark for one who broke my breast.  
I curse thee not with earth above thy head,  
But with the life that never grants thee rest.  

Go, then, beloved traitor—wear thy bloom;  
Dance where the chandeliers like spectres shine.  
Yet in the music’s hush, thy heart shall doom  
Itself to seek a heart as true as mine.  

And finding none, shall love, and love in vain,  
Through wintered years, through nights of weeping stone,  
Till longing is thy chain, remorse thy reign,  
And thou art living—living—and alone.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
